title: Merge sort, LCS and Kruskal's MST
overview: Three classic algorithms close the course. Merge sort shows divide and conquer: split the array in half, sort each half, merge them. Longest common subsequence is a two-string DP. Kruskal's algorithm builds a minimum spanning tree by taking the cheapest edges that do not form a cycle, using DSU. The module's quiz material also contrasts substrings with subsequences.

concepts.explain: Break the problem into halves, solve each half recursively, then combine. For merge sort the combining step is the merge.
Keep one pointer in each array, copy the smaller front element, advance that pointer, and finally copy whatever is left.
log n levels of halving, and each level does O(n) merge work, so O(n log n) time with O(n) extra memory.
A substring is a contiguous block of characters. A subsequence keeps the order but may skip characters. `ace` is a subsequence of `abcde`, not a substring.
Compare the last characters: equal gives 1 + lcs of both shorter strings; different gives the better of dropping one character from either string.
concepts.snippet:
if (a[i] == b[j]) return 1 + lcs(i-1, j-1);
return max(lcs(i-1, j), lcs(i, j-1));

concepts.explain: A set of n-1 edges that connects all nodes with the smallest total weight and no cycle.
Sort edges by weight. Walk through them and keep an edge only if its ends are in different DSU groups; then union them.

files.title: Merge two sorted arrays
files.what: The 'conquer' half of merge sort on its own: merges two sorted arrays into one sorted array with two pointers.
steps: Read sizes `n`, `m` and the two sorted arrays `a`, `b`.
`i`, `j` point into `a`, `b`; `curr` points into the result `c`.
While both have elements, copy the smaller front element into `c` and advance.
Copy the rest of whichever array is not finished.
Print `c`.
files.complexity: Time O(n + m) · Space O(n + m)
files.input_note: n m, then the two arrays, each already sorted.
files.output_note: Prints `1 2 3 4 7 8 9`: every element of both arrays, in order.
files.watch_out: The inputs must already be sorted; merging unsorted arrays gives an unsorted result.

check.q: How many comparisons can merging 4 and 3 elements need at most?
check.a: 6 (n + m - 1), because each comparison places one element and the last one needs no comparison.

files.title: The divide step (splitting only)
files.what: Shows the recursive splitting of merge sort without the merge. It reads an array and halves the range until single elements remain, but prints nothing.
steps: `divide(a, l, r)` stops when `l >= r` (one element or none).
Otherwise `mid = (l + r) / 2`.
Recurse on the left half `[l, mid]` and the right half `[mid+1, r]`.
`main` reads `n m` (m is not used) and the array, then calls `divide(a, 0, n-1)`.
files.complexity: Time O(n) calls · Space O(log n) recursion depth
files.input_note: n and an unused m, then n values.
files.output_note: No output: this file only demonstrates the splitting. Add a `cout << l << " " << r << endl;` at the top of `divide` to watch the ranges.

check.q: For n = 8, how many levels of splitting are there before ranges have size 1?

files.title: Merge sort
files.what: Combines both halves: `divide` sorts the left and right halves recursively and `conquer` merges them back into the original array.
steps: `divide(a, l, r)`: return if the range has one element.
Sort `[l, mid]` and `[mid+1, r]` recursively.
`conquer` copies the two halves into temporary arrays `a` and `b`.
It merges them back into `c[l..r]` with the two-pointer method.
`main` prints the sorted array.
files.complexity: Time O(n log n) · Space O(n)
files.input_note: n and an unused m, then n values (a duplicate 5 is included).
files.watch_out: `main` still reads an unused `m`, left over from `conquer.cpp`; the input must contain it. Using `a[i] <= b[j]` in the merge would make the sort stable (equal values keep their order).

check.q: Why is merge sort always O(n log n), even on already-sorted input?
check.a: It always splits in the middle and always merges, whatever the order of the values.

files.title: Longest common subsequence (memoized)
files.what: Finds the length of the longest subsequence shared by two strings, using `lcs(i, j)` on prefixes `a[0..i]` and `b[0..j]` with a memo table.
steps: `memset(dp, -1, ...)` and read strings `a`, `b`.
Base case: an empty prefix (`i < 0` or `j < 0`) gives 0.
If `a[i] == b[j]`, the answer is `lcs(i-1, j-1) + 1`.
Otherwise the best of skipping `a[i]` or skipping `b[j]`.
Print `lcs(n-1, m-1)`.
files.watch_out: The top comment says 'substring', but the code computes the longest common **subsequence**; a substring version would reset to 0 when characters differ. Tip: on some compilers you need `#include <cstring>` for `memset`; this file relies on another header bringing it in.

check.q: What is the LCS length of `abc` and `def`?

files.title: Minimum spanning tree with Kruskal
files.what: Sorts all edges by weight and greedily keeps each edge that joins two different DSU groups. The sum of kept weights is the MST cost.
steps: Read the edges into `edge_list` as `Edge(a, b, c)`.
`sort` them with `cmp`, cheapest first.
For each edge, find the leaders of both ends.
Different leaders: `dsu_union` them and add the weight to `total_cost`.
Same leader: skip it, it would form a cycle.
Print `total_cost`.
files.complexity: Time O(E log E) · Space O(n + E)
files.input_note: n e, then e edges `a b weight`.
files.output_note: The program crashes before printing anything (status `exit_0xc0000005`, an access violation), and the compiler warns `no return statement in function returning non-void`. That missing `return` is the cause (see Watch out). With the fix it prints `6`: edges 1-2 (1), 3-4 (2) and 1-3 (3).
files.watch_out: `dsu_union` is declared to return `int` but never returns anything. In C++ that is undefined behaviour, and here it makes the program crash on the first union. Make it `void dsu_union(...)`. Also, `memset(group_size, 1, ...)` fills bytes, not ints; set sizes with a loop. If the graph may be disconnected, also count kept edges and check that there are n-1. Tip: on some compilers you need `#include <cstring>` for `memset`.

check.q: Why is it safe to skip an edge whose ends already share a leader?
check.a: Its ends are already connected by cheaper (or equal) edges, so adding it would only create a cycle and raise the cost.

files.title: Sort an Array (practice)
files.what: Sorts an array without the built-in `sort`, which is exactly what this module's merge sort is for. Same `divide` and `conquer` pair as `merge_sort.cpp`, moved into the judge's `class Solution` and working on a `vector` instead of a raw array.
steps: `divide(a, l, r)` stops when `l >= r`: one value is already sorted.
Otherwise split at `mid = (l + r) / 2`, sort `l..mid` and `mid+1..r` by the same call, then merge them.
`conquer` copies the two halves into `left` and `right`, then walks all three with one pointer each, always writing the smaller front value back into `a`.
When one side runs out, the rest of the other side is copied over: it is already in order.
The comparison is `left[i] <= right[j]`, so equal values are taken from the left half first and keep their original order.
`sortArray` just calls `divide` over the whole vector and returns it.
files.complexity: Time O(n log n) · Space O(n)
files.input_note: n, then the n values. The first sample of the problem.
files.watch_out: The left half is `mid - l + 1` values and the right half is `r - mid`, not the same count when the range has an odd length. Slicing with `a.begin() + l` to `a.begin() + mid + 1` gets both sizes right without any arithmetic.

check.q: Why does merge sort cost O(n log n) rather than O(n^2)?
check.a: Halving the range only takes log n levels, and each level merges every value exactly once, which is n work per level.

files.title: Road Reparation (practice)
files.what: Finds the cheapest set of roads that keeps every city reachable from every other city, or prints IMPOSSIBLE. That set is a minimum spanning tree, so this is `mst_using_Kruskal_algorithm.cpp` with the two things the judge needs added: a long long total and a connectivity check.
steps: Read the m roads into a `vector<Edge>` and sort them by cost with the `cmp` comparator.
DSU starts with `par` all -1 (every city is its own leader) and `group_size` all 1.
Walk the sorted roads. If `find(a) != find(b)` the two cities are still in different pieces, so take the road: union them, add the cost, and count it.
If the leaders are already the same, skip the road: it would only close a cycle and cost money for nothing.
`find` sets `par[node] = leader` on the way back (path compression) and `dsu_union` hangs the smaller group under the bigger one, which keeps the trees flat.
At the end a tree over n cities must have exactly n-1 roads. If fewer were taken, the roads left the map in two or more pieces, so print IMPOSSIBLE.
files.complexity: Time O(m log m) for the sort, DSU is near constant per query · Space O(n + m)
files.input_note: n and m, then m lines `a b c`: a road between cities a and b costing c.
files.output_note: Prints `14`. Sorted by cost the roads are 2-4 (2), 1-2 (3), 5-4 (4), 2-3 (5), 5-1 (7), 3-4 (8); the first four join all five cities and add up to 14, the last two would close cycles. On `3 1\n1 2 5\n` it prints `IMPOSSIBLE`, because city 3 has no road.
files.watch_out: Two traps the module's file has. `total_cost` must be a long long: 10^5 roads at 10^9 each overflow an int. And the module's file uses `memset(group_size, 1, sizeof(group_size))`, which fills each byte with 1, not each int; `assign(n + 1, 1)` says what was meant.

check.q: Why is counting the taken roads enough to spot a disconnected map?
check.a: Kruskal takes a road only when it joins two different pieces, so each taken road drops the number of pieces by one. Starting from n pieces, ending with one needs exactly n-1 of them.

recap: Merge sort = split in half, sort both halves, merge with two pointers: O(n log n).
Substring is contiguous; subsequence keeps order but may skip characters.
LCS: equal last characters add 1; otherwise take the better of dropping one side.
Kruskal = sort edges + DSU; keep an edge only when it joins two groups.
An MST of n nodes has exactly n-1 edges.

check_yourself.q: What is the longest common subsequence of `ABCBDAB` and `BDCABA`, in length?
How many substrings does a string of length 4 have (counting repeats)?
Why does Kruskal need the edges sorted?
check_yourself.a: The greedy rule 'always take the cheapest safe edge' only gives the minimum total if edges are considered from cheapest to most expensive.

body: Hand a friend half of an unsorted pile of exam papers, keep the other half, and you both sort your own half. Now two sorted piles lie face up on the table. Joining them is easy: look at the top paper of each pile, take the smaller roll number, repeat. You never look deeper than the top card.
That joining step is the merge, and it is the only clever part of merge sort. Two sorted halves going in:
intro.trace:
left  : 2 5 9        right : 1 6 8

compare      take     result so far
2 vs 1        1       1
2 vs 6        2       1 2
5 vs 6        5       1 2 5
9 vs 6        6       1 2 5 6
9 vs 8        8       1 2 5 6 8
left over     9       1 2 5 6 8 9

body: Every number is copied exactly once, so merging two halves holding n numbers between them costs about n steps.

And if you have no friend? Split your half again, and again, until each pile holds one paper — a pile of one is already sorted. Eight papers split 8, 4, 2, 1: three rounds, and log2 of n rounds in general. Each round merges everything once, about n steps, so the whole sort is O(n log n). For a million numbers that is roughly 20 million steps, where the compare-everything-with-everything sorts of earlier modules would need a million million.

**The second topic is a different animal.** The word `cat` sits inside `cart` if you may skip letters: c, a, jump over r, then t. That is a subsequence. A substring would have to be a solid block, and `cat` is not a solid block of `cart`. The longest common subsequence of two strings is the longest skipping match they share.

Lay the two words out as a table, one down the side and one along the top. Each cell holds the answer for the two prefixes meeting there. If the two letters match, take the cell diagonally up-left and add 1. If they do not match, take the larger of the cell above and the cell to the left — that is "drop a letter from one string or the other, and keep the better result".
intro.trace:
""   c   a   t
   ""      0   0   0   0
   c       0   1   1   1
   a       0   1   2   2
   r       0   1   2   2
   t       0   1   2   3   <- answer

3 letters in common, and they spell "cat"

body: Notice the row for `r`: it matches nothing, so it simply copies the row above. That is the skipped letter.

**The third topic joins villages with cable.** You know the price of every possible cable and want every village connected for the least money. The rule is almost too simple: sort the cables cheapest first, and lay one only if the two villages it joins are not already connected through cables you have laid. If they are, that cable makes a loop — money spent, nothing new reached.

"Already connected to each other" is exactly the question Module 11 answered: `find(a) == find(b)` in a disjoint set union. Kruskal's algorithm is nothing more than that DSU checking a sorted edge list as it goes past. Four villages:

Three edges for four nodes, and that is no accident: a tree that spans n nodes always has exactly n-1 edges. Taking the cheapest edge that is still safe, every time, gives the smallest possible total — which is why this one is called the minimum spanning tree.
The programs below show the splitting and the merging on their own before putting them together as merge sort, then the LCS table, then Kruskal with the DSU written out in full.

walkthrough.heading: Watch it happen: merging two sorted halves
body: The two arrays from `conquer.cpp`: `1 4 7 9` and `2 3 8`, each already sorted. A `^` marks the number each side is currently offering.
One comparison per press. Notice that you never look past the front of either pile - that is why merging n numbers costs about n steps.
walkthrough.frames_title: Press the arrows for one comparison at a time

frames.label: Both pointers start at the front, and the result is empty. The smallest number overall has to be at the front of one pile or the other.
frames.art:
left      1  4  7  9
          ^
right     2  3  8
          ^

compare 1 vs 2

result  (nothing yet)

frames.label: 1 is smaller, so it is copied out and the left pointer steps on. The right pile has not moved.
frames.art:
left      1  4  7  9
             ^
right     2  3  8
          ^

took 1 from the left

result    1

frames.label: Now 4 against 2. The right side is smaller this time, so 2 goes out and the right pointer steps on.
frames.art:
left      1  4  7  9
             ^
right     2  3  8
             ^

took 2 from the right

result    1  2

frames.label: 4 against 3. Right again: 3 goes out. The left pointer has still not moved since the first step.
frames.art:
left      1  4  7  9
             ^
right     2  3  8
                ^

took 3 from the right

result    1  2  3

frames.label: 4 against 8. Left this time, so 4 goes out and the left pointer moves to 7.
frames.art:
left      1  4  7  9
                ^
right     2  3  8
                ^

took 4 from the left

result    1  2  3  4

frames.label: 7 against 8. Left again: 7 goes out.
frames.art:
left      1  4  7  9
                   ^
right     2  3  8
                ^

took 7 from the left

result    1  2  3  4  7

frames.label: 9 against 8. The right side wins its last comparison, 8 goes out, and now the right pile is empty.
frames.art:
left      1  4  7  9
                   ^
right     2  3  8   (all used)


took 8 - right pile is now empty

result    1  2  3  4  7  8

frames.label: One pile is empty, so there is nothing left to compare: the second `while` loop copies whatever the left pile still holds. Seven numbers out for seven steps in, and the result is `1 2 3 4 7 8 9` - exactly what the program prints.
frames.art:
left      1  4  7  9   (all used)

right     2  3  8   (all used)


left over: copy 9 straight across

result    1  2  3  4  7  8  9

walkthrough.heading: Watch it happen: Kruskal picking cables in price order
body: The four villages and five cables from `mst_using_Kruskal_algorithm.cpp`. The rule has only two parts: look at the cheapest cable you have not looked at yet, and lay it **unless** its two villages are already in the same group.
The groups line is the disjoint set union from Module 11 doing its one job: answering `find(a) == find(b)`.
